summary: TiN (111) films grown via plasma-assisted MBE on CO$_2$-laser thermally reconstructed ($\sqrt{31}\times\sqrt{31}$)$R\pm 9°$ sapphire exhibit sharper rocking curves (FWHM $0.048°$ versus $0.098°$) and more isotropic reciprocal-space-map distributions than films on chemically cleaned sapphire, indicating reduced mosaicity and improved crystalline coherence. Superconducting coplanar waveguide resonators fabricated from both film types achieve median internal quality factors $Q_i \approx 1.1$–$1.3\times 10^6$ at single-photon levels ($\langle n \rangle \sim 1$), with many exceeding $10^7$ at higher powers, and comparable superconducting gaps ($\Delta_\mathrm{BCS} \approx 0.63$–$0.67$ meV) and transition temperatures ($T_c \approx 5.08$–$5.11$ K).
motivation: Aggressive chemical preparation of sapphire substrates for epitaxial growth is widely used but involves hazardous solvents; direct thermal laser reconstruction of the c-plane surface into a well-ordered ($\sqrt{31}\times\sqrt{31}$)$R\pm 9°$ reconstruction offers an in-situ, chemistry-free alternative, yet its impact on superconducting device performance remained unexplored.
method: TiN films (106 nm) were grown at $1150°C$ via MBE on both chemically cleaned bare sapphire and on sapphire thermally reconstructed via CO$_2$ laser heating to $1700°C$ for 200 s; crystallinity was assessed by XRD rocking curves, reciprocal-space maps, and TEM cross-sections; superconducting properties were probed by four-point resistivity, STM spectroscopy ($T = 1.2$ K), and cryogenic microwave measurements (down to 20 mK) of $\lambda/4$ CPW resonators on both substrates.
result: Thermally reconstructed sapphire enables TiN films with superior crystalline order (sharper XRD peaks, isotropic strain distribution) while maintaining identical $T_c$, superconducting gap ($\Delta_\mathrm{BCS}$), and residual resistivity ratio ($\mathrm{RRR} \approx 2.6$); resonators on both substrates achieved median $Q_i > 10^6$ at single-photon levels without systematic differences, establishing thermal reconstruction as a viable chemistry-free substrate preparation for superconducting nitride devices.
